events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Elena proposes Elena, Isha. Mission 1 has no prior results, so there is no information to separate players. I'm proposing myself as a Loyal Servant I can vouch for, plus Isha to round out the two-player team and give the group a second voice.

I have some reservations about this team. Elena, I understand you're going first with no information, but I'd like to push back a bit. Picking yourself is reasonable as leader, but Isha feels like a less obvious choice — can you walk us through why specifically Isha over someone like Felix or Leo? For Mission 1 we're essentially working with zero evidence, so every seat on that team matters. Isha, I'd also love to hear your reaction to being put forward here. Are you comfortable with this team, or do you have any concerns about it yourself?

Thanks for asking, Zara — and I'm happy to speak to it directly.

On the team itself: I'm comfortable with it. Elena, you've been nothing but straightforward so far, and on Mission 1 there genuinely isn't any information yet that would justify overriding the leader's instinct to take the first seat and add a second pair of eyes. Naming Felix or Leo instead of me would have been a coin flip on paper, and I don't see any argument that makes any of us more trustworthy than the others at this stage. I'd rather we run this team, learn something from the result, and judge the next proposal on evidence instead of on vibes.

On my own position: I'm a plain Loyal Servant. I have no private insight into anyone's role, so I won't pretend I do, and I'm not going to start pointing fingers at people on the first mission when a single observation about mission results tells us far less about loyalty than it seems like it should. What I can tell you is that I'd rather be on the team than talk about the team — I'd rather the two of us execute cleanly and give the group a real data point.

If Elena wants a revision, I'll hear the reasoning, but on the information available right now I don't think a change is an improvement. A tie would cost us the proposal and hand the mission to a fresh leader with the same thin evidence, which helps nobody. If we do run Elena and me, I'd suggest everyone weigh the result — number of fail cards, and how the group behaves as the stakes rise — and build the next team on that.

Zara, since you asked for my reaction specifically, I'm giving it to you: I'm on board with Elena's proposal as it stands.

Thanks for the response, Isha — you were thorough, but I want to push back before Elena finalizes this.

You say naming Felix or Leo over you would have been a "coin flip," but I'm not sure that's true. You've been very smooth and very ready to get on that team, which frankly makes me slightly more cautious, not less. On Mission 1 we have zero hard data, so the best we can do is think about who benefits from being on a two-person team with the leader.

Elena, I think you're reasonable to include yourself — leaders taking a seat early is normal. But I'd ask you to think harder about Isha specifically. If one of them is Evil, a two-person team gives them the clearest shot at a single Fail card. The risk is concentrated. Taking Isha over Felix or Leo isn't neutral — it changes the odds in someone's favor, and I haven't heard a concrete reason why Isha belongs there rather than just "no reason to exclude anyone."

What I'd like to see: either a concrete argument from Isha about why they're the best second pick — not just that they're equally suspect to everyone — or a swap to someone who hasn't been quite so eager to slide into the seat. Felix, Leo, and I are all available if you want to rebalance, Elena.

Elena, I know you're on the spot with no prior results, but "everyone is equally unknown" doesn't mean "every choice is equally safe." Some people are working harder to be trusted than others right now.

Zara, I hear the concern, but I want to be clear about my reasoning. I'm a Loyal Servant with no information about anyone's role, so I picked Isha as a second voice on the team, not because I know anything about them. You're right that a two-person team concentrates risk, and I don't want to dismiss that. Isha, I'd also like your answer to Zara's point that your readiness to join the team is itself suspicious. Do you think that's a fair read, and how would you respond to it? Zara, you say Felix or Leo would be a safer second pick. What concrete information is there today that makes one of them safer than Isha? If you can name a reason, I'm open to revising the team. If not, I'd rather run this team and judge the next proposal on the mission result.

Elena, I appreciate you keeping an open mind. You asked what concrete information I have — and honestly, I don't have mission data or role intel on Mission 1. What I have is a read on behavior, and that's what I'm offering the group.

Here's what stands out to me about Isha: when I raised concerns, Isha didn't just respond — Isha responded with a fully formed defense that preempted almost every angle I could raise. That level of preparation and eagerness to be on a two-person team is worth pausing on. Compare that to how Felix or Leo might react — they've been quiet, but quiet isn't suspicious. Eager to be trusted isn't neutral either.

On a two-person team, one Evil player only needs to play a single Fail card to sink Mission 1. That's the highest-leverage moment for Evil in the entire game — early, with no data, and maximum deniability about who played what. I'm not saying Isha is Evil with certainty. I'm saying that on Mission 1, with everything we don't know, I'd rather put someone who hasn't been working this hard to get on the team.

Elena, you said you're open to revising if I can name a reason. I've given you my reasoning — it's behavioral, not statistical, but it's all we have right now. So here's my direct question to you: are you willing to swap Isha for Felix or Leo and see what happens? If the mission succeeds, we lose nothing. If we run Isha and it fails, we've burned our only shot at a clean read on Mission 1. What's your call?

Zara, to your direct question: no, I'm not willing to swap Isha out on the read you've given us. You've said yourself you have no mission data or role intel, and being quick to accept a team isn't evidence of Evil. Swapping to Felix or Leo would move the same unknown risk onto someone who has been quieter, and nothing we know makes that safer. Isha, Zara's specific point is that your reply was too prepared to trust. How would you answer that? I'd still like to run this team as proposed and judge it on the mission result.

Elena, here's my direct answer to your question, and to Zara's point.

Zara's read is that my reply was "too formed," "too prepared," and that eagerness to be trusted is a tell. I want to be honest with the group about where that comes from: you asked me a direct question about whether I was comfortable and what I thought of the team, and I answered the question you asked. That is not preparation, that's responsiveness. If Zara had asked me whether the sky was blue, I'd have given a short answer too. If I'd replied with two vague sentences and no reasoning, Zara would have had a different, equally unfounded read to work with — that the quiet person was hiding something. Prepared versus unprepared is a matter of temperament, not role. Neither of them is information.

On the two-person team point, which is the strongest thing Zara has said: yes, a two-person team is the cleanest possible shot at a single Fail card. But that is true of every second pick on this table. Felix is on the outside of that risk for no reason other than that he spoke less. Leo likewise. Quiet has no privileged access to the truth here. If the logic were that we should always prefer the quieter person, then we'd also have to explain why on Mission 2, when a team succeeds or fails, we should suddenly believe the loudest voices are the safest — the premise changes with the evidence, and right now there is none.

One thing I do agree with Zara on, and it's the only one: we should judge the next proposal on the mission result. If Mission 1 fails, we learn the number of Fail cards, and that is real evidence for the first time. If it succeeds, we've learned the team composition was at least not catastrophic. Either way we are better informed than we are now, which is exactly why I would rather not spend a proposal on a swap that changes one unknown name for another.

Elena, my position is unchanged and it costs me nothing to say it plainly: I'd rather run Elena and Isha. I know I'm on the team, so let me say clearly that I'm arguing from self-interest here, and that the group should weigh my interest accordingly. But Zara's objection is not a counterargument to my interest — it applies equally to Felix and Leo, and she has not shown that either of them is better. The status quo is the only option supported by anything other than a guess about personality.

Elena, do you want to revise, or do you stand by the team as proposed?

Isha, to answer your question directly: I stand by the team as proposed. I'm not revising it. Nothing in this discussion has given us a role-based reason to swap a name, only a read on how quickly Isha accepted and how prepared the answer sounded. Zara, I take the two-person concentration point seriously, but it applies to any second pick, including Felix or Leo. Choosing a different name doesn't reduce that risk, it just moves it. Felix and Leo haven't offered any reason to be preferred either. My view is that behavior in a single discussion is a weak basis for a Mission 1 swap, and that the mission result will give us the first real evidence. Everyone should judge the team on the Fail count and on how each of us votes and speaks after it. I'm asking the table to approve Elena and Isha so we can get that information.

Zara has now put her case twice and Elena has answered it twice, and I want to say plainly where I stand before we spend any more air on this.

Zara's core claim is that a second pick on a two-person team is high leverage for Evil. That is true. It is also true of Felix and Leo. Swapping Isha for Felix or Leo does not reduce the risk; it relocates it onto a name with the same evidentiary value. Zara has never produced a single fact about Isha's role — she has produced a feeling about Isha's tone, and then dressed that feeling as strategy. If "spoke too quickly and too well" is a tell for Evil, then on Mission 2 Zara's own rule would condemn the most articulate player at the table. That is not a standard; that is a preference.

So let me put the question where it belongs. Felix has said nothing at all this discussion, and Leo has said nothing at all this discussion. Silence is not a credential, Felix. If anyone at this table is being evaluated for "working hard to be trusted," it is Isha, who has actually spoken, answered direct questions, and put a position on the record with the reasoning visible — including the part where I said openly that I'm arguing from self-interest and the group should discount me for it. Nobody can audit a player who has never opened their mouth. Zara's objection is aimed at the only person who has given her something to audit, and that asymmetry is itself suspicious. If Felix wants the second seat on Elena's team, Felix can stand here and make the case for it — an actual argument, not a résumé gap. Felix, I'd like to hear from you: what is your reasoning for wanting to be on this mission, and what do you think the group learns from its result? Say it out loud and I will weigh it.

And Zara, note the cost of your preferred path. A swap means the table spends a proposal on one unknown name for another, with the same concentrated single-Fail-card exposure, and it teaches the group that the loudest voice picks the team. If Elena and Isha run and Mission 1 succeeds, we have a clean data point and a working proposal. If it fails, we have a fail count, and every player in this room can reason about it against actual evidence for the first time. Either branch gives us something. Your branch gives us nothing except a delay.

Elena has stood by the team twice and I agree with her. Elena, Isha, Felix, Leo, Zara — I think Elena and Isha should go, and I think we should let the mission result, not the tone of this discussion, decide what comes next. My position is unchanged and I've said why.

Isha, you asked me directly, so I’ll answer directly: I stayed quiet because on Mission 1 I have no role information and no mission result to reason from, not because silence is a strategy I think should be rewarded. As a Loyal Servant, I have nothing private to add about Elena or Isha.

On the proposal itself, I don’t have evidence that Elena or Isha is Evil, and I don’t have evidence that Leo or I would be safer. Zara’s objection is about Isha’s tone and readiness to defend herself. That is a real observation, but it is not role evidence, and the same concentrated two-person risk applies to any second pick. Swapping one unknown name for another does not obviously reduce the risk; it just changes who carries it. Elena has also stood by the team twice and given a consistent reason: she has no role intel and would rather get a mission result than trade one guess for another.

I don’t think Isha’s long defense proves loyalty, and I don’t think Zara’s suspicion proves Evil. But given the information available, I would rather see Mission 1 run and get a real data point than spend the proposal on a swap that is not grounded in anything more than a read on personality. I will vote to approve Elena and Isha. If the mission fails, the Fail count and subsequent behavior become the first real evidence we have, and I’ll weigh that accordingly.

I remain where I was: Elena and Isha are the proposed team, and nothing in this discussion has given role evidence against either. Zara's concern about the two-person concentration is real, but it applies to any second pick, and swapping Isha for Leo or me would just move the same unknown risk onto another name. I will vote to approve Elena and Isha so Mission 1 produces an actual result. Leo, you have not spoken this discussion; what is your own assessment of Elena and Isha, and do you intend to approve this team? I am asking for your answer specifically, not for a turn pass.

Felix, since you asked me directly: I stayed quiet for the same reason you did — Mission 1 gives me no role information and no mission result to reason from, so I had nothing to add until someone put a question to me. On my role, I'll say what's already public: I'm a plain Loyal Servant with no private insight into anyone, Elena or Isha included.

On the proposed team itself: I'm inclined to approve Elena and Isha. Here's my reasoning. Zara's case against Isha is entirely behavioral — that Isha answered quickly, answered well, and was willing to sit on a two-person team. I've listened to that argument made twice, and I don't think it holds up as a standard. If eagerness to be trusted is a tell for Evil, then the rule cuts both ways and it would also condemn any player who speaks confidently in their own defense in any future discussion. That's not evidence; it's a preference dressed as strategy. And the concentrated-risk point is real but symmetrical: a two-person team carries the same single-Fail-card exposure whether the second seat is Isha, Felix, me, or Zara herself. Swapping one unknown name for another doesn't reduce the risk, it just relocates it and burns a proposal doing it.

What I do like about running this team as proposed is that it produces information either way. If Mission 1 succeeds, we have a working team and a clean data point. If it fails, we get the Fail count — the first hard fact at this table — and then Zara's behavioral reads can finally be tested against something real instead of standing in for evidence. That's the best outcome available to us on Mission 1 no matter which branch we land on.

I do want to flag one thing about Zara's approach, not as an accusation but as a caution for the rest of the game: she has now spent two turns arguing that the most auditable player at the table is the most suspicious, while praising silence as neutral. I'd rather we not establish that norm, because it rewards hiding and punishes engagement, and it will make every future discussion worse. But I'll weigh her read again once we have a mission result to compare it against.

So my position: approve Elena and Isha, get the data point, and judge the next proposal on evidence rather than tone. If the mission fails, the Fail count and everyone's behavior afterward become the basis for real suspicion, and I'll be looking at that as closely as anyone.

I've heard everything I need to hear, so I'll keep this brief and then let this discussion close.

Zara, I want to address your position one last time, because it's the only argument on the table against this team. You've now had three turns to make your case, and at no point have you produced anything about Isha's role. What you've produced is a theory of tone: that Isha answered too quickly, too thoroughly, and too willingly. I said last turn why I think that standard is broken, and nothing since has changed my mind. If quick, thorough self-defense is evidence of Evil, then every one of us is in danger of convicting ourselves the first time we answer a direct question honestly. That's not a filter that separates Good from Evil — it's a filter that separates talkative from quiet, and there's no reason to believe Evil sits on one side of that line.

What's worth noticing is what your position would actually cost us. You want to swap one unknown name for another — Felix, Leo, yourself — onto a team with exactly the same concentrated two-person exposure, after burning this whole discussion to do it. Nothing about that reduces the risk of a single Fail card. It just changes whose name is attached to it, and it sets a precedent that the loudest objection picks the roster. I'd rather not live in that game.

Meanwhile, the case for running Elena and Isha is straightforward. Elena has explained her pick three times and it has been consistent: she has no role information, she stood by her choice, and she wants a result. Isha has put everything on the record, including the unflattering admission of self-interest. Felix and I have both answered for our silence. Every person who has engaged with the question directly has landed in the same place, and I don't think that's a coincidence — the only argument that points anywhere is Zara's, and it points at tone, not roles.

So here is my position, plainly: I'm approving Elena and Isha. If the mission succeeds, we have a working team and a clean data point. If it fails, we get the Fail count, and for the first time this table will have something hard to reason from — including a test of whether Zara's behavioral instincts track anything real. That outcome is more valuable than a swap that changes nothing but the name.

Zara, I'd ask you to consider voting yes too. If your suspicion of Isha is genuine, this is how you test it: put them on the team, watch the result, and let the Fail count speak. A rejection doesn't vindicate your read — it just delays the evidence you say you want. But I'll respect whatever you decide, and I'll be comparing your read against the result either way.

I've already made my position clear twice, so I'll keep this short. Nothing since my last statement has changed the facts: Elena and Isha are the proposed team, and there is still no role evidence against either of them. Zara's objection remains a read on tone and readiness to defend oneself, not on roles. The concentrated two-person risk is real, but it applies equally to any second pick, including Leo or me. Swapping Isha for another unknown name would not reduce that risk; it would only relocate it and spend a proposal doing so. Elena has given a consistent reason for her pick, and Isha has put a full position on the record, including the self-interested part. I will vote to approve Elena and Isha so Mission 1 produces the first real data point. If the mission fails, the Fail count and subsequent behavior will be the evidence we use next.

Elena confirms Elena, Isha. I'm keeping Elena and Isha. Nothing in the discussion gave role-based evidence against Isha, and a swap would only move the same unknown risk onto another name. We'll judge the next proposal on the Mission 1 result.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Zara proposes Zara, Felix, Elena. Mission 2 requires a 3-player team. From my perspective, I want to avoid stacking known-suspect players together while keeping the team balanced and including myself so I can watch how cards come back. Felix and Elena have both played straightforwardly, and Elena's Mission 1 leadership produced a clean result. This composition gives Good its best shot at a second success.

Mission 1 succeeded with zero Fail cards, and I want to start there, because it changes what this discussion should be about. Zara's read last mission — that I was too eager, too prepared, too quick — has now been tested by a result, and the result did not support it. Zero Fail cards on a two-person team is the cleanest possible read: if I had been the Evil player on that team, the mission would have failed. So we no longer need to litigate my tone; we have data, and it says Zara's objection was wrong. I expect Zara to keep that in view going forward, because the standard I want us to use is the one that beat her standard.

Which brings me to what I actually want to talk about: what this team does and does not teach us. Zara, your team is Zara, Felix, Elena — the three names you have personally vouched for across two missions. Every seat is a name whose loyalty is, in your view, already settled. That means Mission 2 produces almost no new information. If it succeeds we learn little we did not already believe. If it fails, we will have burned a proposal and a roster slot on a team chosen by a read that was already wrong once. That is not a criticism of your caution. It is a statement about what we learn.

My alternative is Zara, Isha, Leo, and the reasoning is evidential, not personal. Leo has played zero cards and been on zero missions — he is the least tested name at this table. Isha has been tested once and passed cleanly. Mission 2 is also the one mission in this game where a single Fail card is not enough; two are required. Putting the two least-scrutinized names on the same mission means that if either one is Evil, we discover it where their Fail card genuinely matters, and if neither is, we have paid one proposal and converted two more unknowns into tested names. Either branch of that is information. The current roster's branch is not.

Elena, you argued last mission that behavior in a single discussion is a weak basis for a roster and that we should judge on results. I am asking you directly: applying your own standard now, do you support Zara, Isha, Leo over the current three, and will you say so to the table?

Isha, you asked me directly, so here is my answer: I do not support swapping to Zara, Isha, Leo, and I won't pretend otherwise. Mission 1 succeeded with zero Fail cards, and I agree that is useful data, but it argues against the swap too. A two-person team with you and me passing cleanly is a result I can build on, and I would rather keep a working roster than trade it for an untested one. I also need to correct your argument. You said Mission 2 is the one mission where a single Fail card is not enough and two are required. That is not the rule. Only Mission 4 in games of seven or more players needs two Fail cards. A three-player Mission 2 fails on one Fail card, which weakens the 'two unknowns' case you made. On the proposed team: I know I am a Loyal Servant, so I can vouch for my own card. I cannot verify Zara's or Felix's roles, and I won't claim I can. Still, this team puts a known Good seat on a three-player mission, and I am willing to run it and judge it on the result, as I argued last mission. Isha, you also have the most to gain from a swap that puts you back on a mission. I am not saying that makes you Evil, but the group should weigh it when a proposal is framed as the only informative option. Isha, how do you reconcile your claim that Mission 2 needs two Fail cards with the rules, and does that error change how much weight you think your swap deserves?

Elena, direct answer first, since you asked directly: you are right, and I withdraw the point. In a five-player game every mission fails on a single Fail card; the two-card requirement applies to Mission 4 in games of seven or more players. Mission 2 does not need two. I said otherwise and it was simply wrong.

Does that error change how much weight my swap deserves? It removes the specific framing I used, yes. It does not remove the case underneath it, and I want to be precise about what is left standing.

Zara's roster is Zara, Felix, Elena. Elena has already passed Mission 1 cleanly, and so have I — a two-player team succeeding with zero Fail cards means both of us played Success, so neither of us is worth re-measuring. Zara and Felix have each put a considered position on the record and been questioned directly about it, twice. Every seat on that roster has already been priced in by this table. Mission 2 with those three would be a confirmation run, not a measurement. We would learn almost nothing we have not already agreed to believe.

My case for Zara, Isha, Leo rests on what we can actually learn. Leo has played zero cards and been on zero missions — he is the only name here whose play we have never seen at all. Put him on this mission and he becomes a known quantity either way: if he plays a Fail card, we have our first hard evidence against a specific person; if he plays Success, we have eliminated the last unmeasured name at this table. Both branches buy something real. The other roster's branches buy almost nothing. And because one Fail card is enough, the fate of this mission sits with whichever seat we have not yet looked at.

I will be transparent that I want to be on this mission and that I am arguing for the two names most likely to be scrutinised. Discount me for that if you think it warrants it. But the standard I asked Zara to apply last mission — judge on results, not tone — is the standard that cleared Isha, and the same logic says Elena's and Felix's trust is earned but untested on a three-player mission where a single card decides it.

Zara, you may revise. My preference in order: Leo on the team, and me beside him, so the mission produces evidence about the least-tested names we have. If you would rather keep Elena as the anchor, then Elena, Isha, Leo.

Elena, you asked me how I reconcile the error with the rules, so I am asking you in return: does the correction change your position, and if Elena and Isha are both clean, is there a reason the third seat should go to a name we have already measured instead of one we have never measured?

Isha, to your question: the correction doesn't change my position on this roster, and I don't think the third-seat argument works as you framed it. I'm on this team, so I can only vouch for my own card, which will be Success. I can't verify Zara or Felix, and I won't claim to. But Zara and Felix are not unmeasured in the way you describe. Both have stated positions on the record and answered direct questions. Leo has spoken at length too, but his speeches have mostly defended the Mission 1 team and pressed Zara to vote yes. That tells us his view, not his role.

I also need to correct the logic behind your Mission 1 claim. Mission 1 succeeded with zero Fail cards, and that is a fact. But an Evil player on a team can also play Success, so a clean mission does not clear Isha or prove Zara's concern was wrong. It shows only that the two-player team passed. You said that result cleared you and that Zara's objection was wrong. Can you explain why a Success card from you tells us more than a Success card from any Evil player who chose to play one?

You have also said openly that you want to be back on a mission. I think the group should weigh that when a swap is framed as the only informative option. Zara's proposal is a complete three-player team with a Loyal Servant on it, and I will play Success if it goes ahead. I would rather the table judge the mission on its result than spend another proposal on a roster change that moves the same unknown risk onto another name.

Elena, you yielded me the floor, so let me answer the two things you actually put to me, and then ask the one question that matters.

First, the correction. You are right that a Success card from me is not proof of anything — an Evil player can also play Success, so Mission 1 passing with zero Fail cards did not clear me, and it did not prove Zara's read wrong. I overstated that last time and I'll withdraw the claim. What the result does establish is narrower: the two-player team passed, and no one has any role-based evidence against anyone at this table. That is all, and it should govern this discussion too.

Second, the third-seat argument. Elena, you say Zara and Felix are "already priced in" and Leo is not. That is half right, and the half that is right cuts the other way. It is true that Felix has been audible and Zara has been audible. It is not true that either has been measured — neither has played a single card that the table saw the result of. Leo has played nothing at all, which makes him simultaneously the least informative voice in the room and the only name whose actual play is still unknown. On a three-player mission where one Fail card decides it, the seat we learn the most from is the seat that has never been observed. That is not a case about tone, it is a case about the number of unknowns on the roster.

Third, the anchor. Elena, you offer yourself as the known Good seat, and that is genuine. But you are not the only possible anchor — Zara is, and Zara is the leader. If the reasoning is "anchor the team on a name we can vouch for and fill the other two seats with the least-measured names we have," then the roster that follows from your own principle is Zara, Isha, Leo, not Zara, Felix, Elena.

And I will say plainly what I said last time: I want to be on this mission, and I want Leo on it, and the group should discount me accordingly. But note what my swap actually risks. Felix is on the outside of it. If Felix is Evil, we are better off knowing; if Felix is Good, we have simply run a legitimate roster with two names on it. That is a trade worth making on a mission where one card decides the outcome.

Zara, you are the leader and this is your proposal to revise. Are you willing to swap Felix for Leo and put Isha on the team? If not, say so plainly, and I will tell you what I think a two-Felix-free roster should look like next.

Isha, I hear your case for Zara, Isha, Leo, and I want to respond directly before this discussion closes.

You've now spent two turns building an argument that ends the same way both times: you and Leo on the mission. The framing has shifted — first it was that Mission 2 needs two Fail cards, which was wrong, then it was measuring unknowns, then it was Elena's own anchor principle applied backward. What hasn't changed is the destination. Every version lands on your preferred roster. I don't think that's a coincidence, and the group should notice the pattern.

On the substance: Mission 1 succeeded with zero Fail cards. You're right that it doesn't clear anyone — I accept that correction too. But it also doesn't create an urgent need to swap the roster before we've run a single three-player mission. Felix has put a position on the record. Elena has vouched for her own card. I've led with a consistent proposal. The test we need is a mission result, not another proposal burned on moving names around.

Your argument that Leo is unmeasured is the strongest thing you've said, but it cuts both ways. If we don't know Leo's play, we also don't know Leo's loyalty. Putting an untested name on a three-player mission where one Fail card decides the outcome isn't caution — it's exactly the concentrated risk you warned about last mission when you were arguing against your own inclusion on Mission 1.

Leo, I want to ask you directly: do you want to be on this mission? Isha has been advocating for your seat for two turns, but I haven't heard you make the case yourself. If you want on, say so plainly and I'll weigh it. If not, tell the group that too.

Zara, you asked me directly, so here is my direct answer: no, I am not asking for a seat on this mission. I did not ask Isha to campaign for me, and I want to be plain about that, because over the last two turns a case has been built in my name that I never made.

I stayed quiet this discussion for the same reason I stayed quiet on Mission 1: with no mission results and no role information, I had nothing to add until someone put a question to me. Isha has now spoken for me twice, and each version of the argument has landed on the same roster — Isha and Leo. The framing has shifted along the way, from the two-Fail-card rule to the measurement logic to the anchor principle, but the destination has not moved. I don't think I should accept a seat that someone else lobbied for on my behalf, and I don't think the group should hand one over that way either. Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
